All organizations are responsible for establishing, promulgating, and maintaining orders of succession to key positions. It is critical to have a clear line of succession to office established in the event leadership becomes debilitated or incapable of performing its legal and authorized duties, roles, and responsibilities. The designation as a successor enables that individual to act for and exercise the powers of a principal in the event of that principal’s death, incapacity, or resignation. Orders of succession enable an orderly and predefined transition of leadership within the organization. Orders of succession are an essential part of a continuity plan and should reach to a sufficient depth and have sufficient breadth—at least three positions deep and geographically dispersed where feasible—to ensure that essential functions continue during the course of any emergency.

In every community, both urban and rural, these societal functions are enabled by infrastructure assets and systems working together to provide critical services.

For example, the public health function relies on electric power to run lights and hospital equipment, clean water for sanitation, emergency services and transportation infrastructure to transport patients and healthcare providers, and many other infrastructure sectors.

Importantly, infrastructure assets and systems not only support societal functions but are also interconnected with and reliant on one another to operate. For example, a community’s water system is almost certainly dependent on electricity to manage filtration processes and power pumps. And electric power generation and transmission systems rely on communication networks to manage, monitor, and control the flow of electricity.
Moreover, many of these systems are large and geographically dispersed, crossing local jurisdictions and state lines and requiring coordination with many partners to enhance resilience.

Rather than treating mergers or closure as the only endpoints for organizations in distress, we found a broad continuum of strategic responses that can preserve — and sometimes strengthen — mission impact under changing conditions.

The first category focuses on making strategic changes to organizational infrastructure, options that allow organizations to continue pursuing their missions while leveraging shared physical, administrative, and programmatic structures.

Two or more organizations [may share space](https://cep.org/blog/going-it-together-three-foundations-one-office/) , staff, technology, or responsibility for designing and carrying out specific programs.
These approaches can reduce overhead burdens and create greater flexibility without requiring organizations to set aside their identities or people.

The second category examines options that involve deeper, often more formal collaboration between organizations. These pathways include fiscal sponsorships, joint ventures, and parent-subsidiary structures.

While these approaches often require significant cultural and governance adjustments, our research suggests they can also reduce competition, consolidate expertise, and improve long-term sustainability when pursued intentionally.

The final category recognizes the reality that exiting may ultimately be the right decision. excerpts: Dissolving an organization can be a difficult and emotional process, but there are steps you can take to ensure that the process of winding down your nonprofit is as smooth as possible.

Whatever the reason to wind down operations, the steps we’ve outlined below will help you plan the process. _Disclaimer: Dissolution is a change in your nonprofit’s corporate status that is governed by state law. We strongly recommend seeking guidance from a lawyer, accountant (regarding final IRS filings), or other professional advisor who has experience with state laws relating to dissolution of tax-exempt organizations and also will be able to guide you through the necessary steps to notify the IRS at the appropriate time that the nonprofit is no longer operating_ . **This article does not constitute legal advice** .

**The board of directors will vote to dissolve the organization, but its job doesn’t end there.** Before making an important decision such as dissolving a nonprofit, the board of directors needs to reach consensus and take an official corporate action (a vote that is documented in minutes of the meeting) to affirm that dissolution is the right path. Usually this is accomplished when the board votes to approve a “plan of dissolution” (which requires that the plan be drafted first! See step #2). The board’s role in deciding whether or not continuing operations is in the best interest of the organization starts long before the plan is drafted, and continues after the vote to adopt the plan.

As you consider the steps below, you should, of course, also consider the impact on the community. There are likely to be volunteers and staff members, board members, and those served by the nonprofit’s mission who will have significant adjustments to make when the nonprofit closes its doors. Additionally, there are likely to be questions about why the organization is winding down, so part of the process will be “managing the message.” Propel Nonprofits’ article [Strategic Sunsetting](https://www.propelnonprofits.org/resources/strategic-sunsetting/) offers good guidance under the section “Communications.”

How the board communicates with the community, employees, volunteers, and other stakeholders (including donors) is important. It may be challenging to balance transparency with respecting confidentiality, but the public will expect the nonprofit’s board to be transparent while also respecting the confidential nature of some financial or personal elements of the winding down process. It is often prudent to [name a spokesperson and establish key agreed-upon talking points](https://nonprofitrisk.org/resources/fact-sheets/communicating-during-a-crisis/) so communications coming from the organization are consistent. (Nonprofit Risk Management Center)
Communicate through designated spokespeople with beneficiaries of the nonprofit’s services so they can make alternative arrangements as far in advance as possible.

Your organization should also inform volunteers, donors, sponsors, and vendors about the decision to wind down. Make sure to provide all donors for the time period prior to closure with gift acknowledgements .
Perhaps another organization is adequately fulfilling the needs that the nonprofit was created to address, or your nonprofit is merging with another nonprofit and will be dissolving as a result.

If the leadership of the organization decides that winding down is the best option, the organization will need a “plan of dissolution.” A plan of dissolution is essentially a written description of how the nonprofit intends to distribute its remaining assets and address its remaining liabilities.

[Federal law requires](https://www.irs.gov/charities-non-profits/charitable-organizations/charity-required-provisions-for-organizing-documents) a tax-exempt charitable nonprofit that is dissolving _to distribute its remaining assets ONLY to another tax-exempt organization_ or to the federal government or a state or local government for a public purpose. Therefore, the dissolution process necessitates identifying other nonprofit(s) or government entity to accept any assets of the dissolving nonprofit.

You will need an inventory of assets to manage this part of the process smoothly. “Assets” could include cash, tangible property such as vehicles or office equipment, and/or intangible property such as data or intellectual property. The transfer of assets may also invoke legal documents such as property deeds, contracts, and trademark registrations. _This means that in the dissolution process your nonprofit cannot give any of its property away to individuals, including board members, other volunteers, employees, or those served_ . excerpts: The [NIST Community Resilience Planning Guide](https://www.nist.gov/topics/community-resilience/planning-guide "NIST Planning Guide") is one resource that outlines a series of basic societal functions that communities provide, such as economic growth, education, and public health.
In every community, both urban and rural, these societal functions are enabled by infrastructure assets and systems working together to provide critical services.

For example, the public health function relies on electric power to run lights and hospital equipment, clean water for sanitation, emergency services and transportation infrastructure to transport patients and healthcare providers, and many other infrastructure sectors.

Importantly, infrastructure assets and systems not only support societal functions but are also interconnected with and reliant on one another to operate. For example, a community’s water system is almost certainly dependent on electricity to manage filtration processes and power pumps. And electric power generation and transmission systems rely on communication networks to manage, monitor, and control the flow of electricity.
Moreover, many of these systems are large and geographically dispersed, crossing local jurisdictions and state lines and requiring coordination with many partners to enhance resilience.

A functional approach begins with understanding what functions are critical to a community or region's success and examines how those functions can be made more resilient. Importantly, this approach does not mean protecting individual assets and systems but instead encourages users to think about how a function can be preserved.
Ultimately, the goal is to limit disruptions to the delivery of essential community functions, whether by reducing the likelihood of infrastructure systems disruptions or reducing their consequences.
For example, while hardening electric grid infrastructure can improve the resilience of community functions, a similar result may be achieved through deploying generators to critical facilities.

T e community land trust (CLT), both the model and the movement, was a long time coming. T e or ga ni za tion generally credited with being the fi rst attempt to cre- ate a CLT, New Communities, Inc., was founded in 1969. Ten years later, only a handful of CLTs were operational in the United States, all of them in remote rural areas. Another 20 years passed before the number, variety, and dispersion of CLTs reached the point where it was fair to speak of a CLT “movement,” although the model’s propo- nents had been brazenly using that term since the early 1980s. Today, there are over 240 CLTs in 45 states and the District of Columbia, and the model has begun spreading to other countries. As long as it took for the model to become a movement, it took even longer for the CLT itself to become the model we know today. New Communities, Inc., did not sud- denly sprout newly green and fully formed from the red clay of southwest Georgia with- out antecedent. It was deeply rooted in a fertile seedbed of theoretical ideas, po liti cal movements, and social experiments that had been laid down over a span of many de- cades. Even after the appearance of New Communities, moreover, this fragile shoot still required years of cultivation and hybridization before it was ready for wider adoption. When laying out the story of the model’s origins and evolution, it is con ve nient to group the distinguishing features of the CLT by own ership, or ga ni za tion, and operation— three clusters of characteristics that appeared at diff erent times, each shaped by a diff erent set of infl uences. excerpts: Dissolving an organization can be a difficult and emotional process, but there are steps you can take to ensure that the process of winding down your nonprofit is as smooth as possible.

Whatever the reason to wind down operations, the steps we’ve outlined below will help you plan the process. _Disclaimer: Dissolution is a change in your nonprofit’s corporate status that is governed by state law. We strongly recommend seeking guidance from a lawyer, accountant (regarding final IRS filings), or other professional advisor who has experience with state laws relating to dissolution of tax-exempt organizations and also will be able to guide you through the necessary steps to notify the IRS at the appropriate time that the nonprofit is no longer operating_ . **This article does not constitute legal advice** .

**The board of directors will vote to dissolve the organization, but its job doesn’t end there.** Before making an important decision such as dissolving a nonprofit, the board of directors needs to reach consensus and take an official corporate action (a vote that is documented in minutes of the meeting) to affirm that dissolution is the right path. Usually this is accomplished when the board votes to approve a “plan of dissolution” (which requires that the plan be drafted first! See step #2). The board’s role in deciding whether or not continuing operations is in the best interest of the organization starts long before the plan is drafted, and continues after the vote to adopt the plan.

As you consider the steps below, you should, of course, also consider the impact on the community. There are likely to be volunteers and staff members, board members, and those served by the nonprofit’s mission who will have significant adjustments to make when the nonprofit closes its doors. Additionally, there are likely to be questions about why the organization is winding down, so part of the process will be “managing the message.” Propel Nonprofits’ article [Strategic Sunsetting](https://www.propelnonprofits.org/resources/strategic-sunsetting/) offers good guidance under the section “Communications.”

How the board communicates with the community, employees, volunteers, and other stakeholders (including donors) is important. It may be challenging to balance transparency with respecting confidentiality, but the public will expect the nonprofit’s board to be transparent while also respecting the confidential nature of some financial or personal elements of the winding down process. It is often prudent to [name a spokesperson and establish key agreed-upon talking points](https://nonprofitrisk.org/resources/fact-sheets/communicating-during-a-crisis/) so communications coming from the organization are consistent. (Nonprofit Risk Management Center)
Communicate through designated spokespeople with beneficiaries of the nonprofit’s services so they can make alternative arrangements as far in advance as possible.

Your organization should also inform volunteers, donors, sponsors, and vendors about the decision to wind down. Make sure to provide all donors for the time period prior to closure with gift acknowledgements .
Perhaps another organization is adequately fulfilling the needs that the nonprofit was created to address, or your nonprofit is merging with another nonprofit and will be dissolving as a result.

If the leadership of the organization decides that winding down is the best option, the organization will need a “plan of dissolution.” A plan of dissolution is essentially a written description of how the nonprofit intends to distribute its remaining assets and address its remaining liabilities.

[Federal law requires](https://www.irs.gov/charities-non-profits/charitable-organizations/charity-required-provisions-for-organizing-documents) a tax-exempt charitable nonprofit that is dissolving _to distribute its remaining assets ONLY to another tax-exempt organization_ or to the federal government or a state or local government for a public purpose. Therefore, the dissolution process necessitates identifying other nonprofit(s) or government entity to accept any assets of the dissolving nonprofit.

You will need an inventory of assets to manage this part of the process smoothly. “Assets” could include cash, tangible property such as vehicles or office equipment, and/or intangible property such as data or intellectual property. The transfer of assets may also invoke legal documents such as property deeds, contracts, and trademark registrations. _This means that in the dissolution process your nonprofit cannot give any of its property away to individuals, including board members, other volunteers, employees, or those served_ . The nonprofit can, however, sell its assets, as long as the individual or entity purchasing the asset is paying a reasonable amount, ideally the “fair market value.” Start with an inventory of assets, then plan which assets will be sold/transferred/contributed. Some assets may require external appraisals/valuations, while the monetary value of others will be straightforward. Don’t overlook trademark registrations as a potential asset that need to be transferred. Document all transfers and sales, noting the fact that transfers of assets are only to other entities with tax-exempt public charity designation (501(c)(3)) or to a federal/state/tribal/local government.

It is key that all remaining assets be distributed in a manner that is consistent with 1) federal and state law, 2) your organization’s bylaws or articles of incorporation, and 3) the plan of dissolution.

Schedule N requires a dissolving nonprofit to report **a** **description of the assets, the date of distribution, the fair market value of the assets, and information about the recipients of the assets** , so Schedule N serves as a good guide for what details need to be documented by the organization as it is distributing its assets.

The way to [inform the IRS of the organization’s dissolution](https://www.irs.gov/charities-non-profits/termination-of-an-exempt-organization) is by filing the organization’s final IRS Form 990 (and 990-T if applicable).
Submit [Schedule N](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f990sn.pdf) , which documents the tax-exempt entity(ies) to which your organization is transferring its remaining assets.

All of your nonprofit’s liabilities, including taxes, need to be identified. Don’t forget future contractual obligations. Next, make a plan to pay off current debts and terminate recurring or future liabilities. (Some nonprofits have future restricted revenue or future liabilities on their books. This is where the expertise of an accountant may be needed!). Determine whether all of these obligations can be satisfied by existing cash or whether some assets need to be sold to pay the liabilities. If your organization cannot satisfy its debts and has insufficient remaining assets, [bankruptcy](https://nonprofitquarterly.org/2014/04/29/nonprofit-corporation-navigating-through-bankruptcy/) might be the best option. Final financial statements should reflect no remaining liabilities (or assets).

Eventually, a “certificate” or “articles of dissolution” will be filed with the state agency that handles corporate registrations. Filing a plan of dissolution notifies the state of incorporation of the organization’s plans to dissolve.

The organization is not officially dissolved until the dissolution papers are filed with the state, and other final steps, such as filing the final annual report (Form 990) with the IRS, are completed.

**STEP #6 Notify Other State Agencies** Once the Articles/Plan of Dissolution is filed with the state, contact state authority(ies) to inform those offices that the nonprofit is no longer operating. State agencies that may be relevant for your nonprofit include the Attorney General or other state charity official that regulates charitable solicitation registration, the state taxation office, state department of labor (if the nonprofit had employees), and any state licensing authorities, such as department of health or human services, that may have accredited or licensed the nonprofit’s activities. Larger workplaces may have obligations under state WARN laws (Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification). **Step #7 Notify the IRS** The next step is to let the IRS know that the organization is officially dissolved in its state of incorporation. The way to [inform the IRS of the organization’s dissolution](https://www.irs.gov/charities-non-profits/termination-of-an-exempt-organization) is by filing the organization’s final IRS Form 990 (and 990-T if applicable). The Form 990 is due within 5 months and 15 days after the last day of the organization’s most recently completed fiscal year, but if a nonprofit closes its doors mid-year, it can file the 990 as soon as it has completed all the state dissolution requirements, even if the fiscal year is not yet over. Form 990-N filers should file a final 990-N for the most recently completed fiscal year.

**Step #2 Drafting the Plan of Dissolution** If the leadership of the organization decides that winding down is the best option, the organization will need a “plan of dissolution.” A plan of dissolution is essentially a written description of how the nonprofit intends to distribute its remaining assets and address its remaining liabilities. Eventually, a “certificate” or “articles of dissolution” will be filed with the state agency that handles corporate registrations. Filing a plan of dissolution notifies the state of incorporation of the organization’s plans to dissolve. **Practice pointers** The state may provide a template form that the nonprofit can use as its official plan of dissolution (such as this [very basic plan of dissolution from](https://www.ilsos.gov/publications/pdf_publications/nfp11220.pdf) Illinois) Your organization’s plan should include all the assets and liabilities you can identify and describe how liabilities will be satisfied, which nonprofits will receive the remaining assets, and the fair market value of those assets. It’s a good idea for the board to also document who will be responsible for what, and by when, in order to maintain accountability throughout the dissolution process. excerpts: The [NIST Community Resilience Planning Guide](https://www.nist.gov/topics/community-resilience/planning-guide "NIST Planning Guide") is one resource that outlines a series of basic societal functions that communities provide, such as economic growth, education, and public health.
In every community, both urban and rural, these societal functions are enabled by infrastructure assets and systems working together to provide critical services.

For example, the public health function relies on electric power to run lights and hospital equipment, clean water for sanitation, emergency services and transportation infrastructure to transport patients and healthcare providers, and many other infrastructure sectors.

Importantly, infrastructure assets and systems not only support societal functions but are also interconnected with and reliant on one another to operate. For example, a community’s water system is almost certainly dependent on electricity to manage filtration processes and power pumps. And electric power generation and transmission systems rely on communication networks to manage, monitor, and control the flow of electricity.
Moreover, many of these systems are large and geographically dispersed, crossing local jurisdictions and state lines and requiring coordination with many partners to enhance resilience.

A functional approach begins with understanding what functions are critical to a community or region's success and examines how those functions can be made more resilient. Rather than treating mergers or closure as the only endpoints for organizations in distress, we found a broad continuum of strategic responses that can preserve — and sometimes strengthen — mission impact under changing conditions.

The first category focuses on making strategic changes to organizational infrastructure, options that allow organizations to continue pursuing their missions while leveraging shared physical, administrative, and programmatic structures.

Two or more organizations [may share space](https://cep.org/blog/going-it-together-three-foundations-one-office/) , staff, technology, or responsibility for designing and carrying out specific programs.

The second category examines options that involve deeper, often more formal collaboration between organizations. These pathways include fiscal sponsorships, joint ventures, and parent-subsidiary structures.

Whatever the reason to wind down operations, the steps we’ve outlined below will help you plan the process. _Disclaimer: Dissolution is a change in your nonprofit’s corporate status that is governed by state law. We strongly recommend seeking guidance from a lawyer, accountant (regarding final IRS filings), or other professional advisor who has experience with state laws relating to dissolution of tax-exempt organizations and also will be able to guide you through the necessary steps to notify the IRS at the appropriate time that the nonprofit is no longer operating_ . **This article does not constitute legal advice** .

**The board of directors will vote to dissolve the organization, but its job doesn’t end there.** Before making an important decision such as dissolving a nonprofit, the board of directors needs to reach consensus and take an official corporate action (a vote that is documented in minutes of the meeting) to affirm that dissolution is the right path. Usually this is accomplished when the board votes to approve a “plan of dissolution” (which requires that the plan be drafted first! See step #2). The board’s role in deciding whether or not continuing operations is in the best interest of the organization starts long before the plan is drafted, and continues after the vote to adopt the plan.

As you consider the steps below, you should, of course, also consider the impact on the community. There are likely to be volunteers and staff members, board members, and those served by the nonprofit’s mission who will have significant adjustments to make when the nonprofit closes its doors. Additionally, there are likely to be questions about why the organization is winding down, so part of the process will be “managing the message.” Propel Nonprofits’ article [Strategic Sunsetting](https://www.propelnonprofits.org/resources/strategic-sunsetting/) offers good guidance under the section “Communications.”

How the board communicates with the community, employees, volunteers, and other stakeholders (including donors) is important. It may be challenging to balance transparency with respecting confidentiality, but the public will expect the nonprofit’s board to be transparent while also respecting the confidential nature of some financial or personal elements of the winding down process. It is often prudent to [name a spokesperson and establish key agreed-upon talking points](https://nonprofitrisk.org/resources/fact-sheets/communicating-during-a-crisis/) so communications coming from the organization are consistent. (Nonprofit Risk Management Center)
Communicate through designated spokespeople with beneficiaries of the nonprofit’s services so they can make alternative arrangements as far in advance as possible.

Your organization should also inform volunteers, donors, sponsors, and vendors about the decision to wind down. Make sure to provide all donors for the time period prior to closure with gift acknowledgements .
Perhaps another organization is adequately fulfilling the needs that the nonprofit was created to address, or your nonprofit is merging with another nonprofit and will be dissolving as a result.

If the leadership of the organization decides that winding down is the best option, the organization will need a “plan of dissolution.” A plan of dissolution is essentially a written description of how the nonprofit intends to distribute its remaining assets and address its remaining liabilities.

The transfer of assets may also invoke legal documents such as property deeds, contracts, and trademark registrations. _This means that in the dissolution process your nonprofit cannot give any of its property away to individuals, including board members, other volunteers, employees, or those served_ . T e community land trust (CLT), both the model and the movement, was a long time coming. T e or ga ni za tion generally credited with being the fi rst attempt to cre- ate a CLT, New Communities, Inc., was founded in 1969. Ten years later, only a handful of CLTs were operational in the United States, all of them in remote rural areas. Another 20 years passed before the number, variety, and dispersion of CLTs reached the point where it was fair to speak of a CLT “movement,” although the model’s propo- nents had been brazenly using that term since the early 1980s. As long as it took for the model to become a movement, it took even longer for the CLT itself to become the model we know today. New Communities, Inc., did not sud- denly sprout newly green and fully formed from the red clay of southwest Georgia with- out antecedent. It was deeply rooted in a fertile seedbed of theoretical ideas, po liti cal movements, and social experiments that had been laid down over a span of many de- cades. Even after the appearance of New Communities, moreover, this fragile shoot still required years of cultivation and hybridization before it was ready for wider adoption. When laying out the story of the model’s origins and evolution, it is con ve nient to group the distinguishing features of the CLT by own ership, or ga ni za tion, and operation— three clusters of characteristics that appeared at diff erent times, each shaped by a diff erent set of infl uences. T e reality was much messier, of course, with ideas often leapfrogging the narrative boundaries between eras.

Rather than treating mergers or closure as the only endpoints for organizations in distress, we found a broad continuum of strategic responses that can preserve — and sometimes strengthen — mission impact under changing conditions.

Two or more organizations [may share space](https://cep.org/blog/going-it-together-three-foundations-one-office/) , staff, technology, or responsibility for designing and carrying out specific programs.

The second category examines options that involve deeper, often more formal collaboration between organizations. These pathways include fiscal sponsorships, joint ventures, and parent-subsidiary structures.

It also has the advantage that it can be terminated, or its terms modified, if the CLT finds it is not working as intended. The major disadvantage is that, on a day-to-day basis, a separate entity is inserted between the CLT and its constituents (tenants and perhaps ground lessees) and may not be as responsive to those constituents as the CLT would like.

_Transfer of real property assets by a CLT that will continue to exist_ . While continuing to operate as an independent organization, a CLT may transfer ownership of some or all of its real estate to one or more entities. A CLT might, for instance, transfer all of its rental property to to another entity with existing rental management capacity while continuing to own and steward land beneath owner-occupied CLT homes. Or it might choose to transfer all real property assets while continuing to operate other programs such as housing-related training programs or neighborhood planning and advocacy programs. In any transfer of property, the CLT will be concerned with seeing that the transferee has both the capacity to carry out necessary stewardship functions and a commitment to doing so for the long term. Dealing with Worst Cases 09/1011 12 In any such transactions, the transferee will need to accept responsibility for all mortgage debt secured by the transferred properties, and will need to agree to use the properties in accordance with the terms of any subsidies invested in them. And the holders of all such mortgages and the sources of all such subsidies will have to consent to the transfers in question. The legal work required to see that all responsibilities are formally transferred and that all necessary parties have given written consent may take time and may entail significant expense. The CLT will need to work closely with its attorney to complete the process, The primary advantage of this approach is that, while retaining the ability to carry out certain functions such as educational, planning, and advocacy activities, the CLT is able to pass on to a more qualified institution a set of stewardship responsibilities that it does not have the capacity to carry out. The primary disadvantage is that, unless the transferee is itself a CLT with a proven track record, it will be hard to be sure of the long-term capacity and commitment of that institution (whose bylaws are unlikely to contain the kinds of permanent stewardship requirements that are typical of CLT bylaws). It should also be emphasized that the legal process entailed by this approach is much more extensive and complicated than what is entailed by a contract for services.

_Merger with another not-for-profit corporation._ A CLT may arrange to merge its assets, liabilities and corporate identity with those of another 501(c)(3) charitable corporation, on terms and conditions agreed to by both parties. In recent years a variety of nonprofit housing organizations have merged with others. Some of them have been relatively strong organizations seeking to gain further strength and sustainability through economies of scale. ... substantially compromising their (presumably similar) missions. For a CLT exploring merger possibilities with a different sort of nonprofit – perhaps a more conventional sort of housing organization or CDC – one crucial question will be how willing that organization is to accommodate the CLT’s mission, governance principles, and client relationships. Obviously, the more dissimilar the two organizations are the more problematic a merger will be. The task of negotiating and implementing any merger will necessarily require much work and much time. It is also likely to involve some painful personnel decisions as the two organizations become one. _Restructuring as an affiliate of another not-for-profit corporation_ . While retaining a separate identity and board of directors, a CLT may be restructured (under new or revised bylaws) to give another nonprofit corporation some degree of control over it. The most extreme form of restructuring can establish the other organization as the sole “member” of the CLT with the right to appoint all members of the CLT’s board – the CLT thus becoming, in effect, a “subsidiary” of the other organization. Classic CLTs, with their very different and distinctive membership structures, will normally want to resist giving up this much control over their board composition. However, a CLT that has stopped growing, and therefore no longer experiences the excitement of new projects, can find it difficult to sustain enough energy at the board level to support effective governance. This sort of loss of momentum can be self-perpetuating. At a certain point, a subsidiary relationship with a stronger organization may be the best way for such a CLT to see that necessary stewardship activities will continue to be carried out. For CLTs less in need of a major infusion of new leadership, a less extreme form of restructuring may be appropriate.

T e community land trust (CLT), both the model and the movement, was a long time coming. T e or ga ni za tion generally credited with being the fi rst attempt to cre- ate a CLT, New Communities, Inc., was founded in 1969. Ten years later, only a handful of CLTs were operational in the United States, all of them in remote rural areas. Another 20 years passed before the number, variety, and dispersion of CLTs reached the point where it was fair to speak of a CLT “movement,” although the model’s propo- nents had been brazenly using that term since the early 1980s. Today, there are over 240 CLTs in 45 states and the District of Columbia, and the model has begun spreading to other countries. As long as it took for the model to become a movement, it took even longer for the CLT itself to become the model we know today. New Communities, Inc., did not sud- denly sprout newly green and fully formed from the red clay of southwest Georgia with- out antecedent. It was deeply rooted in a fertile seedbed of theoretical ideas, po liti cal movements, and social experiments that had been laid down over a span of many de- cades. Even after the appearance of New Communities, moreover, this fragile shoot still required years of cultivation and hybridization before it was ready for wider adoption. When laying out the story of the model’s origins and evolution, it is con ve nient to group the distinguishing features of the CLT by own ership, or ga ni za tion, and operation— three clusters of characteristics that appeared at diff erent times, each shaped by a diff erent set of infl uences. T e reality was much messier, of course, with ideas often leapfrogging the narrative boundaries between eras.

content.cep_s_mission_continuity_makes_nonprofit:
The closest direct nonprofit precedent is the Center for Effective Philanthropy's mission-continuity framework. CEP organizes options into infrastructure changes, deeper collaboration, and strategic exit. Its infrastructure category lets organizations share space, staff, technology, or responsibility for programs without necessarily abandoning their identities or people [cep_s_mission_continuity_makes_nonprofit_exit_transferable[0]] [11]. Its collaboration category includes fiscal sponsorships, joint ventures, and parent-subsidiary structures [cep_s_mission_continuity_makes_nonprofit_exit_transferable[0]] [11].

The decisive overlap is the exit category. CEP expressly identifies mergers, acquisitions, and transfer of programs or assets to peers as ways to preserve mission while an organization winds down [cep_s_mission_continuity_makes_nonprofit_exit_transferable[0]] [11]. It states that an organizational ending does not necessarily mean that the mission has failed [cep_s_mission_continuity_makes_nonprofit_exit_transferable[0]] [11]. It also says organizations should engage these questions throughout their life cycles rather than waiting for a financial or other crisis [cep_s_mission_continuity_makes_nonprofit_exit_transferable[0]] [11]. That combination contains four core elements of the candidate: a nonviability or closure trigger, advance consideration, separation of mission from the corporation, and transfer to other institutions.

The National Council of Nonprofits turns that principle into a closure workflow. It says leaders should consider community impact and communicate with beneficiaries early enough for them to make alternative arrangements [cep_s_mission_continuity_makes_nonprofit_exit_transferable[1]] [9]. It describes a dissolution plan as a written account of asset distribution and liabilities, and tells organizations to inventory assets and decide which will be sold, transferred, or contributed [cep_s_mission_continuity_makes_nonprofit_exit_transferable[1]] [9]. Federal charitable restrictions also require remaining assets to go to another tax-exempt organization or a government entity, which makes identifying a receiving institution part of the dissolution process [cep_s_mission_continuity_makes_nonprofit_exit_transferable[1]] [9].

New York's Attorney General guidance adds a formal recipient-screening layer. A board-approved plan must address assets and liabilities, and proposed recipient organizations should conduct substantially similar charitable activities and document their legal status and compliance with restrictions [cep_s_mission_continuity_makes_nonprofit_exit_transferable[2]] [6]. But the limits are equally important: the guidance does not impose specific program continuity, client-notice, records-preservation, or pre-nonviability planning requirements [cep_s_mission_continuity_makes_nonprofit_exit_transferable[2]] [6].

**Decision insight:** Nonprofit practice creates a strong target-domain root collision. The residual is not "preserve the mission after closure" in general; it is a member-level, function-by-function plan that identifies receiving capacity for housing, care, food, records, transport, and other dependencies before the crisis.
content.clt_dissolution_clauses_preserve_housing:
Community land trusts provide the clearest housing-specific precedent. The CLT Technical Manual says a CLT seeking 501(c)(3) status must restrict asset distribution upon dissolution [clt_dissolution_clauses_preserve_housing_beyond_the_corporation[0]] [13]. It then describes more specific bylaws that may direct land to another community land trust, or, if no such CLT is able and willing to assume ownership, to an organization whose purposes include long-term preservation of affordable access to land and housing for low-income people [clt_dissolution_clauses_preserve_housing_beyond_the_corporation[0]] [13].

That is a structural separation between the legal entity and the housing function. The corporation may dissolve, but the land and its affordability purpose are not treated as ordinary residual property. The manual also says a CLT may turn all assets over to a single nonprofit or government entity capable of using the real estate and other assets consistently with the CLT mission [clt_dissolution_clauses_preserve_housing_beyond_the_corporation[0]] [13]. It qualifies the mechanism: the receiving organization must have both the capacity to perform necessary stewardship and a long-term commitment to doing so [clt_dissolution_clauses_preserve_housing_beyond_the_corporation[0]] [13].

The routine CLT model reinforces the same logic before dissolution. The manual describes the CLT as having ongoing responsibility to the community for the care of land and housing [clt_dissolution_clauses_preserve_housing_beyond_the_corporation[0]] [13], and says it must be prepared to carry out effective stewardship on a truly perpetual basis [clt_dissolution_clauses_preserve_housing_beyond_the_corporation[0]] [13]. This is not merely a liquidation rule. It is a governance technology for making a physical and social function outlast the current organization.

The limitation is scope. The manual's dissolution and stewardship provisions address land, housing, and affordability. It does not, in the cited material, provide one integrated continuity plan for care, food, records, transport, communications, or other member-critical functions. It also presents dissolution alternatives and restructuring options rather than a universal requirement that every CLT maintain a fully specified successor playbook [clt_dissolution_clauses_preserve_housing_beyond_the_corporation[0]] [13].

**Decision insight:** The housing portion of the candidate is not original at the level of mechanism. The defensible contribution is to extend CLT-style successor stewardship from land and housing to a coordinated portfolio of member-critical functions and to make the trigger and handoff operationally explicit.
content.confidence_and_search_limitations:
**Confidence in the root collision: high.** The CEP framework directly addresses strategic closure and preserving mission through transfers [confidence_and_search_limitations[0]] [11]. The CLT manual directly addresses successor stewardship of land and housing [confidence_and_search_limitations[1]] [13]. Federal residential-care rules directly address transfer of residents after provider-agreement termination [confidence_and_search_limitations[2]] [10]. These are target-domain precedents, not merely analogies from computing or corporate disaster recovery.

**Confidence in the narrow residual: medium-high.** NIST, CISA, and the California nonprofit template supply the multi-function, dependency, records, alternate-site, and recovery vocabulary [confidence_and_search_limitations[3]] [8][confidence_and_search_limitations[4]] [17]. GEN supplies an intentional-community resilience research program but does not show the institutional-death handoff [confidence_and_search_limitations[5]] [1]. The residual is therefore supported as an integration gap, but not proven to be globally absent.

Important limitations remain. Public intentional-community governance documents are unevenly available, and a private community may have a succession or dissolution plan that is not indexed or public. The search located credible resilience work in intentional communities, but not a publicly documented plan that combines the candidate's full set of functions. Nursing-facility materials are sector-specific; nonprofit dissolution rules vary by jurisdiction; and the Consumer Voice recommendations are a documented proposal rather than proof that every jurisdiction implements them. The NY AG guidance expressly does not supply all program, client, records, or advance-contingency requirements [confidence_and_search_limitations[6]] [6].

The conclusion is not that no stronger precedent exists. It is that the strongest located evidence defeats a broad originality claim while leaving a precise, potentially useful residual: a member-centered, pre-event, cross-function successor protocol for a community whose institution may cease to exist.

**Decision insight:** Retain the candidate only under the narrow residual framing, and cite nonprofit mission continuity, residential closure transfer, and CLT successor stewardship as its established roots.
content.fema_s_essential_functions_doctrine_stop:
The candidate has a recognizable two-track structure. Track one asks whether the institution can preserve leadership, authority, facilities, data, and operating capacity. Track two asks whether the functions that members depend on can continue even if the institution cannot. The important originality question is therefore not whether anyone has used the words "continuity" or "essential functions." It is whether the target domain already transfers member-serving functions away from a failing entity through a predefined architecture.

FEMA's Continuity Guidance Circular is the strongest formal source-domain root. It defines continuity planning around an organization's essential functions and requires capabilities that operate under a wide range of emergencies [fema_s_essential_functions_doctrine_stops_at_reconstitution[0]] [7]. It calls for orders of succession, including at least three positions deep where feasible, so essential functions can continue when leaders are unavailable [fema_s_essential_functions_doctrine_stops_at_reconstitution[0]] [7]. It also recognizes devolution: essential functions and leadership authorities can move to a safe and secure location with trained personnel [fema_s_essential_functions_doctrine_stops_at_reconstitution[0]] [7].

The boundary matters. FEMA defines reconstitution as recovery from an emergency and restoration of operations and resources so the organization returns to full operation [fema_s_essential_functions_doctrine_stops_at_reconstitution[0]] [7]. Its continuity model is therefore primarily an organization-preservation model. Devolution changes location or leadership; it does not, in the cited guidance, dissolve the institution and assign housing, care, food, records, or transport to independent successor providers. FEMA's public toolkit likewise defines continuity as uninterrupted critical services while maintaining organizational viability [fema_s_essential_functions_doctrine_stops_at_reconstitution[1]] [5].

NIST and CISA extend the grammar from organizations to communities. NIST asks planners to establish desired recovery times for essential community functions and to identify dependencies among social institutions and the built environment [fema_s_essential_functions_doctrine_stops_at_reconstitution[2]] [8]. CISA says the planning focus should be preservation of a critical function rather than protection of an individual asset [fema_s_essential_functions_doctrine_stops_at_reconstitution[3]] [2]. These are important conceptual precedents, but they remain source-domain or community-infrastructure frameworks unless paired with target-domain evidence about an institution's failure and successor transfer.

**Decision insight:** The candidate should not claim the essential-functions idea, devolution, or function-first planning as novel. Its defensible residual begins where standard continuity planning stops: permanent institutional nonviability and member-facing handoff.
content.gen_s_20_ecovillage_resilience_program_l:
The strongest intentional-community-specific item located is the Global Ecovillage Network's Ecovillage Resilience and Resilience 2.5 work. GEN frames the project around whether ecovillages can survive and thrive through climate change, a 2.5-degree scenario, and polycrisis [gen_s_20_ecovillage_resilience_program_leaves_a_transfer_gap[0]] [1]. It reports participation by **20 ecovillages across 18 countries** from 2022 to 2024 and describes the work as a research and learning experiment intended to support reflection and practice [gen_s_20_ecovillage_resilience_program_leaves_a_transfer_gap[0]] [1].

GEN Europe's project update says participating ecovillages examined resilience attributes, defined as features that help a system respond to disturbances, stresses, and shocks [gen_s_20_ecovillage_resilience_program_leaves_a_transfer_gap[1]] [3]. The public outputs include an online course in three languages, a podcast, companion cards, case studies, resilience stories and tips, and a resilience tracker [gen_s_20_ecovillage_resilience_program_leaves_a_transfer_gap[0]] [1]. This makes the program credible target-domain research rather than a generic business-continuity analogy.

But the public description does not specify the candidate's key transfer mechanism. It does not state that an ecovillage should predefine what happens when its legal or governing institution becomes nonviable. It does not identify successor organizations or alternate providers for housing, care, food, records, transport, or communications. Nor does it present a two-lane operating model that distinguishes restoration of the community institution from continuation of member-critical functions. Those are absences from the located description, not proof that no participating ecovillage has private documents containing them.

This distinction protects the originality claim from two opposite errors. It would be too strong to say that intentional communities have no resilience planning; GEN is clear evidence that they do. It would also be too strong to say that GEN has already established the candidate's architecture; the cited project description does not show that. The search also did not locate a credible, public intentional-community plan with the complete institutional-death and multi-function handoff structure.

**Decision insight:** The intentional-community residual is real but narrow. The candidate can contribute a specific failure-mode protocol to a field that already has resilience language and practice, but it cannot claim novelty for community resilience itself.

| California nonprofit continuity and recovery template | Nonprofit survival, operations, people, facilities, and records | It asks nonprofits to identify critical operations, essential records, offsite copies, alternate locations, chain of command, restart procedures, and full restoration procedures [nist_cisa_and_california_map_multi_function_continuity[2]] [17] | It is a disaster continuity and recovery template, not a permanent nonviability or successor-provider plan |
| FEMA CGC 1 | Essential functions and organizational continuity | It provides succession, delegations, devolution, continuity facilities, and reconstitution [nist_cisa_and_california_map_multi_function_continuity[3]] [7] | Its endpoint is restoration of the organization, not independent continuation of member functions |

The table shows why the candidate feels familiar without being fully anticipated. NIST and CISA supply the dependency map. California supplies a target-domain nonprofit worksheet for records, alternate sites, and recovery. FEMA supplies authority and devolution mechanics. None of these sources, alone, says: if this member-serving institution cannot continue, transfer each function to a named alternate while separately deciding whether the institution itself will recover.

**Decision insight:** The multi-function inventory is a synthesis opportunity, not a blank slate. Originality is available in the crosswalk that connects function dependencies, receiving providers, records custody, resident choice, and organizational recovery status.
content.nursing_facility_closure_turns_resident_:
Residential care provides the most concrete operational analogue. Under 42 CFR 488.426, the state may transfer Medicaid and Medicare residents to another facility in an emergency, or close the facility and transfer those residents [nursing_facility_closure_turns_resident_care_into_a_transfer_duty[0]] [10]. When the state or CMS terminates the provider agreement, the state must arrange the safe and orderly transfer of all covered residents to another facility, with notification handled under the referenced closure rules [nursing_facility_closure_turns_resident_care_into_a_transfer_duty[0]] [10].

This is more than ordinary disaster preparedness. The institution's regulatory status can end, yet the resident-serving obligation persists through a receiving facility. The architecture therefore separates the provider entity from the resident function. It supplies a predefined trigger, a responsible public actor, and an alternate institution. In candidate terms, it directly covers institutional nonviability or closure, continuity of care as a resident-serving function, and transfer to a successor setting.

The National Consumer Voice study makes the architecture more resident-centered. It recommends a coordinated state closure team and a closure protocol that defines the roles of the state, closing facility, receiving facility, residents, and families [nursing_facility_closure_turns_resident_care_into_a_transfer_duty[1]] [12]. It recommends keeping a facility open until residents are transferred to an appropriate location of their choosing and continuing public payments until successful relocation [nursing_facility_closure_turns_resident_care_into_a_transfer_duty[1]] [12]. Its discharge-planning recommendation includes a meeting at least **14 days** before the move and counseling on how the resident, records, and belongings will be moved, with written meeting notice at least **7 days** in advance [nursing_facility_closure_turns_resident_care_into_a_transfer_duty[1]] [12].

The study also requires attention to resident choice, quality, services, location, and best interests [nursing_facility_closure_turns_resident_care_into_a_transfer_duty[1]] [12], and says that an inventory of possessions should accompany the resident to the new home [nursing_facility_closure_turns_resident_care_into_a_transfer_duty[1]] [12]. That is a useful operational precedent for records and transport, not just abstract continuity. It also exposes a limitation: the federal rule is specific to covered nursing-facility residents, and the study is a closure proposal for long-term care. Neither source creates a general community protocol for food systems, shared housing, transport, or records outside the care episode.

**Decision insight:** Residential-care practice is a near-direct collision for the closure trigger and the resident handoff. The candidate's residual is broader system composition: one plan that coordinates care transfer with housing, food, records, transport, and member governance rather than treating them as a single regulated service.
content.synthesis_preserve_the_integration_aband:
Across mechanism, scope, trade-offs, evidence base, and time horizon, the precedents converge on a clear result. FEMA and California continuity guidance are organization-centered and event-oriented: they preserve essential operations, authority, records, alternate sites, and eventual restoration [synthesis_preserve_the_integration_abandon_broad_originality[0]] [7][synthesis_preserve_the_integration_abandon_broad_originality[1]] [17]. NIST and CISA are community-function-centered and infrastructure-oriented: they identify lifelines, dependencies, and recovery performance, but do not establish a successor for a failed private institution [synthesis_preserve_the_integration_abandon_broad_originality[2]] [8][synthesis_preserve_the_integration_abandon_broad_originality[3]] [2].

The target-domain practices add the missing transfer logic in separate sectors. CEP and nonprofit closure guidance distinguish mission from the original corporation and identify peers or public entities that can receive programs or assets [synthesis_preserve_the_integration_abandon_broad_originality[4]] [11][synthesis_preserve_the_integration_abandon_broad_originality[5]] [9]. Nursing-facility closure practice protects residents through a receiving facility, resident choice, records, belongings, and closure roles [synthesis_preserve_the_integration_abandon_broad_originality[6]] [10][synthesis_preserve_the_integration_abandon_broad_originality[7]] [12]. CLT practice protects housing stewardship by directing land to another CLT or a mission-compatible organization with capacity and long-term commitment [synthesis_preserve_the_integration_abandon_broad_originality[8]] [13].

The non-obvious tension is that each precedent solves only one side of the problem. Nonprofit law protects charitable assets but does not guarantee that clients receive uninterrupted programs. Nursing-home rules protect residents but operate within a specialized regulatory and payment system. CLT clauses protect land and affordability but do not protect care, food, records, or transport. GEN's ecovillage program is closer in social setting, but its public account remains resilience-oriented rather than institution-death-oriented [synthesis_preserve_the_integration_abandon_broad_originality[9]] [1].

That makes the proposed architecture a credible residual if it is stated narrowly. A community could define, before crisis, a function register; a nonviability threshold; a recovery lane for the legal organization; a continuity lane for each member-critical function; named alternate providers or successor entities; records custody; resident/member choice; asset and contract transfer; and tests or review cycles. The recommendation is to describe this as a cross-domain synthesis inspired by established practices, not as an unprecedented discovery.

**Final disposition: ROOT COLLISION + NARROW RESIDUAL.** The root proposition is already established in the target domain: mission, resident care, and housing stewardship can continue through another institution after the original organization closes. No located source, however, directly combines the full candidate architecture for an intentional or residential community across housing, care, food, records, transport, and other functions while separately tracking organizational recovery.
